rules_text:
Rules summary Contents 1 How to play 1.1 Setup 1.2 Gameplay 1.3 Beasts 1.4 Tokens 1.5 Winning and Losing How to play Setup Lay out the three spaces for the hundreds, tens, and ones digits on the table. Shuffle the "Beast" cards into the main deck, with the number of beasts determining the difficulty. Deal each player five cards. Gameplay On your turn, choose one suit and play all the cards of that suit from your hand to the table. You can play the cards in any order you choose, but the number formed by the digits must be higher than the previous number. For example, if the number is 275, you could play an 8 to make 278, 285, or 875. Cards have a suit (clubs, spades, hearts, diamonds) and a variety ("broken" or "whole"). Broken cards have a golden shape around their suit symbol and whole cards don't. Both suit and variety together form a card's type. Communication is limited. You can say things like "I can help," but you cannot show your cards or reveal their suit numbers or varieties. Beasts When a "Beast" card is played, it is placed above the 1s place. The Beast blocks that type (suit + variety) from being played in the column directly beneath it. If the space beneath the Beast has a card of the same type as the Beast, the Beast is "startled" and moves to the next column to the left that does not contain a card of the same type as the Beast. If all cards are the same type as the Beast, it has been "defeated/captured" and is removed from play. Tokens You can use one of your three discard tokens at any time during your turn to discard a non-Beast card from your hand. Winning and Losing You win if the team plays all the cards from the deck. You lose if you cannot play a card and a player still has cards in their hand.

community_text:
[Rating: 1/10] The visual design is an active pain, I can't tell if a beast is blocking the normal or cracked version of a card, so it takes me twice as long to figure out what I can do on my turn. Once I got over that hurdle... it's just an optimization game, where we had no reason to communicate with each other. So it's twice as complex as The Game, with half the co-op. Plus that awful rulebook to get through.

[Rating: 4.75/10] The difficulty seems luck dependent and there is no meaningful player communication (or really much to communicate).  The cards are beautiful, which makes the gameplay that much more disappointing.

[Rating: 5/10] It was nice to play but lasted a bit long for what it was. Could do with some more player agency.

[Rating: 5/10] The game looks great and is fairly simple.  However, it is also pretty boring.  I also wish the beasts themselves stood out a bit more.  I didn't hate the game, but it is not something I would rush back to.

[Rating: 5/10] Grundsätzlich ok, aber das Regelheft muss dringend überarbeitet werden. Ich bin mir immer noch nicht sicher ob bei BGA noch ein Bug ist oder ob ich einfach nur regeltechnisch etwas nicht verstanden habe. Grundsätzlich erwarte ich aber auch nicht das eine Klarstellung des Regelheftes meine Meinung zum Spiel in irgendeiner Weise verbessert.

[Rating: 6/10] Light little co-op filler that I enjoy. A good one to play while having a conversation.

[Rating: 6/10] Based on 1 play with 4 players and 4 beasts: This was a fun-enough puzzle but I'm always skeptical of a co-op game we win on the first go. Not only did we win, we came away with a sweet 992 points.  It's nice that there are difficulty levers here and I will experiment with them, but I always find a sandbox of difficulty levers less compelling than a set of authored difficulty levels... it just feels like work to have to come up with my own rubric and then I don't have that immediate pull to come back and see if I can beat "the next level." I like feeling like there's a meta challenge to overco

[Rating: 6/10] Took much of the game to figure out the rules, but that might have been the other three players all trying to teach me at the same time.
